title: Remote Access Tools: IDE Tunneling
summary: IDE tunneling is the narrow case of the remote access parent where the channel is provided by an integrated development environment. Modern editors bundle secure shell connectivity, port forwarding, file synchronisation and remote debugging into one session, and several of them also ship a command-line tunnel command that registers the machine with the vendor's relay and returns a public web address for it. That relay makes the technique unusually quiet on the network side, because the outbound connection is transport-encrypted and terminates at a domain that belongs to a legitimate software vendor, and the operator can authenticate with an ordinary developer account rather than a stolen credential for your estate. The behaviours that matter are the tunnel client running on a host that has no developer role, workspace or server configuration files that contain remote connection details and auto-launch the editor at logon, and inbound use of the generated web address. Because the parent technique covers remote access generally, the distinguishing feature here is the development toolchain itself acting as the transport and the identity provider: the adversary blends into a workflow that already expects encrypted outbound connections, frequent file transfer and command execution. Detection works best on host telemetry, where tunnel process creation, its arguments, and the editor or helper binary that survives a reboot stand out against a software inventory, supplemented by DNS and proxy logs for vendor tunnel endpoints on machines that should never contact them.

beginner.definition: Developers often use an editor program that can work on a computer somewhere else. The editor builds a secure tunnel, which is a private path over the internet, and keeps the files and the terminal in step. Attackers can use the same editor and the same tunnel to get a remote session on your machine.
beginner.whyItMatters: This differs from the general remote access idea because the tunnel is made by a tool developers already use every day. The traffic looks like normal development work and goes to a well-known software company, not to an unknown server. The attacker may log in with a normal developer account, so there is no broken password to notice. On most business computers no editor should be running at all, which is exactly why its presence is a useful signal.
howItWorks: The attacker installs or uses an editor that supports remote development on the compromised computer.
They run the editor's tunnel command, or configure a workspace file that starts one automatically.
The editor's helper connects out to the vendor's relay service and registers the machine.
The relay returns a web address, and the attacker opens it to reach the machine's terminal and files.
The attacker may add the editor to the startup list so the tunnel is rebuilt after every restart.
From the tunnel they can use the machine as a jump host and reach other systems in the network.
beginner.example: Think of a building with a service entrance used by the same repair company every week. The guards know the van, the paperwork is in order, and the workers sign in as usual. One week a van from that company arrives with a crew that was never requested, parks in the service bay, and stays for days. The van is genuine and the paperwork checks out, but nobody asked whether a repair was booked at all.
takeaways: Encrypted traffic to a trusted vendor can still be an unauthorised remote session.
A development tool running on a business computer with no developer role is a strong warning sign.
Check editor settings and startup entries for tunnels that reconnect by themselves.

objectives: Explain what IDE tunneling provides beyond plain secure shell and port forwarding.
Describe how a tunnel client registers a machine with a vendor relay and returns a web address.
State how this sub-technique differs from the general remote access parent technique.
Identify host and network telemetry that reveals an unauthorised development tunnel.
Explain how auto-launch settings turn a tunnel into a persistent access method.
